children: By Fergal Smith

Canada's main stock index was barely changed on Monday as declines for metal mining shares offset gains for energy and technology, with investors growing cautious ahead of an expected U.S. Federal Reserve interest rate hike this week.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index
ended up 5.04 points, or 0.01%, at 35,702.53, remaining above the near six-week low it posted on Thursday.

"With a potential U.S. Fed interest rate increase looming on Wednesday and concerns surrounding the AI sector increasing, stock markets are mixed globally and retreating in the U.S. to start the new trading week," Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management, said in a note.
Wall Street dipped after top executives in U.S. artificial intelligence companies raised safety concerns and called for a slowdown in the development of AI.
In domestic data, the consumer price index rose 3% year-over-year in August, matching expectations but remaining well above the Bank of Canada's 2% target.
BoC Governor Tiff Macklem has said that policymakers were prepared to raise borrowing costs multiple times if inflation remained too high.
The materials group
, which includes metal mining shares, fell 2.3% as gold
and copper (HGc1) prices declined on increased bets that the Fed will tighten on Wednesday.
S&P Dow Jones is expanding the eligibility criteria for S&P/TSX Canadian indices in a move that investors say could allow for the inclusion of copper producer Anglo-Teck.
Most other sectors ended higher, including energy
, which added 0.7%
U.S. crude oil futures
settled 1.3% higher at $101.39 a barrel as worries about energy supplies mounted following new strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and attacks on ships in the Middle East.
Shares of Thomson Reuters
rose 8.9%, which helped lift the industrials sector (.GSPTTIN) by 1%.
Technology
added 0.8%, with Constellation Software
up 4.7% and e-commerce company Shopify
adding 4.4%.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is welcoming dozens of global investors to Toronto, hoping to lure investments for more than 160 projects that he says are key to steering Canada's economy through a trade war with the United States.
